soil-agri-039.title: Soil remineralization: feeding fields with rock dust
soil-agri-039.text: A dressing of crushed rock can feed a field for up to 5 years. Soil remineralization replenishes a soil's mineral nutrients by working rock powder into it. Multi-nutrient rock fertilizers release potassium, calcium, magnesium and some phosphorus slowly, mimicking the natural weathering of parent material. Plants take what they need and the rest stays crystallized, whereas unabsorbed soluble fertilizer salts run off to groundwater. Combined with organic fertilizer, rock powder has matched chemical fertilizer at much lower cost. It also raises soil pH and can use local mining waste. The limits are real. It needs heavy application rates and releases nutrients slowly, so it cannot replace industrial fertilizers. Dissolution depends on organic matter, pH and the formation of secondary clays, and lab rates can be 2–5 orders of magnitude higher than field rates. Some volcanic and phosphate rocks contain toxic, heavy or radioactive elements. One prospect draws wider interest. Cations released from some powders react with carbon dioxide to form carbonate minerals, which could help mitigate global warming.

soil-agri-137.title: Do organic fields end up with better soil?
soil-agri-137.text: Whether organic farming leaves a soil better off is still disputed. Supporters say organic soil has higher quality and holds more water, which may help yields in drought years. A 2007 USDA study found that manure in tilled organic systems built soil better than {{ref:soil-agri-117}}. Yet an 18-year study on nutrient-depleted, cold-temperate soils found conventional methods better for fertility and yield, crediting organic gains to imported materials. Gunsmoke Farms, a 137 square kilometre organic project in South Dakota, suffered massive erosion from turning the soil after converting.

soil-agri-136.title: How organic farms keep their soil fertile
soil-agri-136.text: Without synthetic fertilizer, an organic farm has to grow and recycle its own nutrients. Organic soil fertility management replaces what crops remove through the natural breakdown of organic matter, using green manure and composting. Soil organisms such as mycorrhiza and earthworms release the nutrients to plants through the growing season. Supplying nitrogen when crops need it most is the hard part; legumes in rotations and green manures fix it with rhizobia. Farmers also use animal manure, seed meal and mineral powders such as greensand and phosphate rock. Farms without livestock struggle more and rely on imported manure, which is bulky and costly to haul far.

soil-agri-051.title: Basin irrigation: flooding a level plot
soil-agri-051.text: Some fields are watered by filling them like a shallow pool. Basin irrigation quickly floods a level area enclosed by earth banks and leaves the water to soak in. It is favoured on soils with relatively low infiltration rates, and traditional basins are not drained afterwards. Laser levelling and land grading now allow large rectangular basins suited to mechanised broadacre cropping. In drainback level basins, water passes from each bay to a lower one in turn, a layout common in Australian rice and wheat rotations.

soil-agri-050.title: Furrow irrigation: water down the rows
soil-agri-050.text: Furrow irrigation sends water by gravity from the top of a field down small parallel channels that follow its main slope. Furrows run from under 100 to 2,000 m long and suit row crops such as cotton, maize and sugar cane. The water's speed depends above all on the inflow rate and the soil's infiltration rate. A slow advance soaks the top end more than the bottom; a faster one improves uniformity and cuts the water needed. Surge irrigation pulses the flow on and off, sealing the surface so the water advances faster.

soil-agri-052.title: Spate irrigation: catching the desert flood
soil-agri-052.text: In dry lands, river beds that sit empty most of the year sometimes carry floods for hours or days. Spate irrigation diverts these seasonal floods onto fields or into storage basins. It is an ancient method of arid and semi-arid lands in the Middle East, North Africa, West Asia, East Africa and parts of Latin America. Intakes, spurs or bunds send the water through channel networks to command areas from a few hectares to over 25,000 ha. Fast floodwater moves large amounts of sediment, so river banks and beds can change rapidly.

soil-agri-045.title: Fallow syndrome: the hungry crop after a rest
soil-agri-045.text: Resting a field can leave the next crop hungry. Fallow syndrome is poor nutrient uptake by a crop after a fallow period. The soil lacks arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi, root partners that help plants take up nutrients. Any plant roots, even those of weeds, reduce its occurrence. Susceptible crops such as corn should therefore follow a crop that hosts the fungi, such as oats or another small grain, rather than a fallow. Fields are now routinely sown with {{ref:soil-agri-066}} to prevent erosion, suppress weeds, supply green manure and lower the risk of fallow syndrome.

soil-agri-043.title: Holistic planned grazing and the carbon dispute
soil-agri-043.text: Holistic planned grazing keeps livestock herds rotating between fields to mimic how natural herds graze. Trampling is reported to aid soil restoration, plant regrowth, carbon storage and water infiltration. How much carbon it stores is disputed. A meta-analysis of studies from 1972 to 2016 found it no better than continuous grazing for plant cover and biomass. A 2016 Swedish study put the realistic rate of carbon storage seven times lower than Allan Savory's claims. Adaptive multi-paddock grazing, by contrast, has done less damage to soil than continuous grazing.

soil-agri-134.title: Alley cropping: crops in the lanes between trees
soil-agri-134.text: Alley cropping grows strips of crops between rows of closely spaced trees or hedges. The trees are pruned before the crop is planted, and the cut leaves are spread over the crop area to supply nutrients. The hedges also shelter the crop from wind and reduce erosion. Leguminous Inga trees suit the method well. They fix nitrogen, grow on acid tropical soils, and drop a thick mulch that protects the soil and shades out weeds. Inga alley cropping lets land be cultivated repeatedly, an alternative to slash-and-burn farming. In the temperate strip-cropping variant, trees grow in wide strips rather than single rows.

soil-agri-037.title: Rock phosphate: phosphorus straight from the quarry
soil-agri-037.text: Much conventional fertilizer added to phosphorus-deficient soils turns into insoluble complexes, so it has to be reapplied constantly. Rock phosphate fertilizer uses phosphorite, a phosphorus-bearing sedimentary rock, as a sustainable, low-cost source of phosphorus. Its phosphorus must be processed before plants and soil can take it up. Fungi can do this by producing organic acids. Industry grinds the rock, adds water and sulfuric acid, removes impurities as gypsum, then treats the acidic liquid with ammonia vapour to make granules. A study in Zimbabwe found that mining dust mixed with processed fertilizer raised plant growth, phosphorus levels and organic carbon.

soil-agri-057.title: Zaï: planting pits that revive dry land
soil-agri-057.text: A shallow pit can multiply a harvest. Zaï is a farming technique of digging pits in poorly permeable soil to catch water and concentrate compost. The pits are 15 to 50 cm across and 5 to 15 cm deep, spaced about 80 cm apart. Farmers in the western Sahel have traditionally used it to restore degraded dry land and raise fertility, and it has spread to semi-arid East Africa. From the 1980s, filling the pits with manure and compost was reintroduced. This attracts termites, whose tunnels break up the soil, and yields of trees, sorghum and millet can rise by up to 500 percent.

soil-agri-035.title: Biosolarization: compost speeds the sun's work
soil-agri-035.text: Biosolarization adds compost or other organic amendments to soil before solarizing it, so that microbial activity shortens the treatment. It is an alternative to soil fumigation, closely related to soil solarization and to {{ref:soil-agri-056}}. All of them use solar heat or plant chemistry against nematodes, bacteria, fungi and other pests. Spanish research on strawberry production found it sustainable and cost-effective, and small farms in California use it. It can double as organic waste management, and food-industry residues can make it more efficient.

soil-agri-132.title: Deficit irrigation: watering less on purpose
soil-agri-132.text: Deficit irrigation deliberately gives a crop less than its full water needs. It waters during the drought-sensitive growth stages and limits water at other times. The aim is the highest crop water productivity, the marketable product per cubic meter of water, rather than the highest yield. Cotton irrigation in Turkey and India could be cut to up to 60 percent of the crop's water requirement with limited yield loss. Maize, sensitive all season, suffers. Less nutrient leaches, but the risk of salinization is higher than under full irrigation.

soil-agri-056.title: Biofumigation: plants that gas soil pests
soil-agri-056.text: Mustard can do a fumigant's job. Biofumigation is pest control in which a fumigant gas comes from fresh plant material chopped and buried in the soil to decompose. Brassicas such as mustard, cauliflower and broccoli release isothiocyanates from their glucosinolates. These are toxic to soil bacteria, fungi and nematodes but less persistent than synthetic fumigants. Sorghum releases hydrogen cyanide instead. The plants are chopped at flowering and worked into soil irrigated to field capacity, then covered with film for three or four weeks. The method can also replenish nutrients, but it is slow and hard to standardize, because cultivars differ in active content.

soil-agri-031.title: Soilless substrates that hold roots in hydroponics
soil-agri-031.text: In hydroponics, plants grow without soil, but their roots still need something to grip. Soilless growing substrates are inert or organic materials such as perlite or gravel that support the roots mechanically. Rock wool, spun from molten basalt or slag, is the most widely used, though its naturally high pH needs conditioning. Expanded clay pellets, fired at 1,200 °C until they swell and turn porous, are inert, pH-neutral and light. Coir swells three to four times when wet but must first be washed of salts, tannins and phenolics. Perlite holds more air and less water than vermiculite.

soil-agri-131.title: Center-pivot irrigation: watering in circles
soil-agri-131.text: A standard 400-meter center-pivot machine waters about 50 hectares in one circle. Center-pivot irrigation sprinkles a circular area of crop from a line of pipe on wheeled towers that rotates around a central pivot. Drops hang the sprinklers a few feet above the crop to limit evaporation and wind drift. The system needs less working of the soil than ground irrigation, reducing runoff, erosion and compaction. But decades of pumping have emptied parts of the Ogallala Aquifer, where the water table has dropped more than 1.5 m per year in places.

soil-agri-011.title: Variable rate application: changing the dose as you go
soil-agri-011.text: A GPS-guided spreader can raise or lower its fertilizer rate as it crosses a field, because nutrient needs differ with soil properties and sunlight. Variable rate application applies a material such as fertilizer at a rate that changes with the location or qualities of each part of a field. It is either map based, following prescription maps an advisor prepares in advance, or sensor based, calculated in real time on the applicator. Electromagnetic induction, considered cost-effective and non-destructive, can make the maps. Varying the rates of nutrients or pesticides can cut their use, saving costs and reducing harmful runoff into waterways.

soil-agri-033.title: Sheets, vacuums and sandwiches: ways to steam soil
soil-agri-033.text: Steam can be pushed into soil from above, drawn down from below, or both. Soil steaming methods fall into substrate, surface and deep soil steaming, chosen by soil structure, crop and area to treat. Sheet steaming treats 15 to 400 m2 at once, reaching 25–30 cm depth and 90 °C in 4–5 hours. Vacuum depth steaming draws steam down through pipes and penetrates best, reaching up to 80 cm with fixed drainage pipes. Sandwich steaming pushes steam in from the surface and from depth at once. Stack steaming treats compost and substrates piled up to 70 cm high.

soil-agri-025.title: Salinity classes: matching salty soils to crops
soil-agri-025.text: Bernstein graded soils by how salty they are and what will still grow in them. His classes use ECe, the electrical conductivity of a saturated soil-paste extract, in decisiemens per metre. ECe 0–2 is non-saline. From 2–4 the soil is slightly saline, and sensitive crops lose yield. From 4–8 it is moderately saline. From 8–16 it is saline, and only tolerant crops yield normally. Above 16, only very tolerant crops do. Soil salinity control draws different bounds, calling soil saline only above ECe 4. Schleiff ranks crop tolerance in narrower 2 dS/m steps than the 4 dS/m steps in Richards' 1954 USDA handbook.

soil-agri-027.title: Crops that tolerate seawater
soil-agri-027.text: Certain varieties of potato, carrot, red onion, white cabbage and broccoli thrive when watered with salt water, Dutch trials found. Crop tolerance to seawater is a crop's ability to withstand irrigation with seawater or a mix of fresh water and seawater. Salt Farm Texel tests crops on 56 plots of 160 m2 at seven salt levels, from EC 2 to 35 dS/m. The levels are made by mixing fresh water with seawater of about 50 dS/m. Thresholds varied widely even within one crop: potato ranged from 1.9 dS/m for the variety Met to 4.1 dS/m for Mignonne.

soil-agri-003.title: Agroecosystems: the ecosystems people farm
soil-agri-003.text: A farm is an ecosystem with a manager. An agroecosystem is an ecological system that people manage and shape in order to farm. Researchers study its system properties: productivity, stability, sustainability and equitability. Harper's 1974 concept of agroecosystems, perhaps inspired by Tansley's process ecology of the 1930s, is considered the foundation of modern {{ref:soil-agri-002}}. Some losses are permanent. Erosion can irreparably reduce an agroecosystem's productive capacity, and {{ref:soil-agri-066}} are often grown for that reason alone.

soil-agri-002.title: Agroecology: ecology applied to farming
soil-agri-002.text: Basil Bensin used the word agroecology in 1928, according to Wezel and colleagues; another account credits the German zoologist Friederichs. Agroecology is an academic discipline that studies ecological processes as they apply to agricultural production systems. Tischler's 1965 book Agrarökologie may be the first with the word in its title. Today the term can mean a science, a movement or a farming practice, and it is not tied to any single method, whether organic, regenerative, integrated or industrial. It draws on the sciences to study soil properties and plant-insect interactions, and on the social sciences to study farming's effects on rural communities. Ecosystem agroecology treats farms as integrated ecological systems, analysing their energy flows and nutrient cycles. As practice, it harnesses biodiversity, nutrient recycling, {{ref:soil-agri-140}}, intercropping and composting. Its certified forms are biodynamic farming, organic agriculture and China's Green Food. Its politics are unsettled. Researchers debate heatedly which model of agriculture policy should support, and the UN is perhaps agroecology's most prominent backer.

reviews.farming-systems-and-growing-media: Irrigation lifts yields, but every method, from basins and furrows to sprinklers and drip lines, has to balance water against loss. Too much water leaches nitrate and phosphorus or raises salty water tables, and too little lets salts build up at the surface, which is why salt tolerance and efficiency matter so much. Crop choices pull the same way: rotations, fallows, intercropping and mixed farming spread crops through time and space, countering the depleted nutrients and adapted pests of monocropping. Organic and regenerative farming lean on compost, manure and legumes, though how much they help soil and climate is still disputed. Even the media and treatments, from coir and potting mixes to steaming and solarization, serve the field's long aim of keeping soils productive.
